{{Short description|Ancient Greek mathematician (1st century AD)}}
{{about|the 1st century AD mathematician|the 3rd century BC mathematician|Dionysodorus of Caunus}}
'''Dionysodorus of Amisene''' (1st century AD) was a Greek mathematician from [[Pontus (region)|Pontus]], now on the [[Black Sea]] coast of [[Turkey]]. He was briefly described by [[Strabo]], as one of the learned men of the city of Amisus.<ref name=mactutor/><ref name=strabo/> Despite the similarity of his demonym to the inland city of [[Amaseia]], where Strabo was born, translators H. C. Hamilton and W. Falconer instead footnote Amisus as being the modern city [[Samsun]], near Amaseia on the coast. Amisene is a name for the region containing both cities.<ref name=strabo/>

Strabo distinguishes him from Dionysodorus of Melos, a geometer,<ref name=strabo>{{citation|url=https://archive.org/details/geograofstrablit02strauoft/page/296|translator1-first=H. C.|translator1-last=Hamilton|translator2-first=W.|translator2-last=Falconer|title=The Geography of Strabo, Literally Translated, With Notes|publisher=H. G. Bohn|location=London|year=1854–1857|page=296}}</ref> whom [[Pliny the Elder]] describes as having calculated the circumference of the Earth, less accurately than the older calculation of [[Eratosthenes]]. He should also be distinguished from  [[Dionysodorus|Dionysodorus of Caunus]], who studied [[conic section]]s.<ref name=mactutor>{{mactutor|id=Dionysodorus|title=Dionysodorus}} Primarily about Dionysodorus of Caunus, but briefly notes the Dionysodorus of Pliny's account, and states that [[Strabo]] distinguished Pliny's Dionysodorus from Dionysodorus of Amisene.</ref>

Dionysodorus of Amisene was long thought to be the Dionysodorus who studied conic sections until, in the early 20th century, {{ill|Wilhelm Crönert|de}} found from a papyrus newly excavated at [[Herculaneum]] a connection from the study of conics to Dionysodorus of Caunus and his son, also named Dionysodorus, dating them to centuries before the time that Strabo wrote about.<ref name=mactutor/><ref>{{citation|first=Thomas|last=Heath|author-link=Thomas Heath (classicist)|title=A History Of Greek Mathematics, Volume II: From Aristarchus to Diophantus|publisher=Clarendon Press|year=1921|location=Oxford|page=218|url=https://archive.org/details/historyofgreekma029268mbp/page/218}}</ref>
